props.title: Pulp Fiction

sections.content: **Pulp Fiction** (1994) revolutionized American independent cinema with its nonlinear storytelling and pop culture-soaked dialogue. Tarantino's masterpiece weaves three interconnected crime stories that shattered conventional narrative structure. The film's influence echoes through countless imitators like **Go** (1999) and **Things to Do in Denver When You're Dead** (1995), but none matched its electric chemistry between John Travolta and Samuel L. Jackson or its ability to make mundane conversations about foot massages and hamburgers crackle with tension.

sections.content: The film's impact on 90s cinema can't be overstated. It spawned an entire subgenre of interweaving crime narratives like **2 Days in the Valley** (1996) and **Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels** (1998). But Pulp Fiction's real genius lies in its ability to subvert expectations - making audiences laugh at violence one moment and squirm in discomfort the next. The famous "gold watch" monologue by Christopher Walken demonstrates how Tarantino can turn a simple backstory into riveting cinema.

Beyond its narrative innovation, **Pulp Fiction** (1994) revitalized careers and launched new ones. It resurrected John Travolta from direct-to-video obscurity, cemented Samuel L. Jackson as a leading man, and proved Uma Thurman could carry dramatic weight. The film's success also enabled a wave of independent filmmakers like Robert Rodriguez (**From Dusk Till Dawn** (1996)) and Roger Avary (**Killing Zoe** (1993)) to secure funding for their own crime-soaked visions. movies.title: Natural Born Killers
movies.slug: Oliver Stone directs Tarantino's script about two lovers on a murder spree, with a savage take on media sensationalism

sections.content: Pulp Fiction sparked a renaissance in stylized crime films throughout the 1990s. Works like **The Usual Suspects** (1995) and **Fargo** (1996) brought fresh approaches to familiar genres. The film's DNA is evident in later works like **Seven** (1995) and **L.A. Confidential** (1997), which similarly play with narrative convention while exploring the darker corners of criminal life.
